Even if you are using a secure email provider, since the app runs on your phone, all of the data that passes in and out of it is ultimately at the device maker's disposal.

This is partially mitigated by running a custom ROM on your phone, but even then the baseband or Trusted Execution Environment is still running highly-privileged, proprietary code. The same is essentially true for all computers, until we have truly open source hardware.

Anything you type will always be available to the os due to the hooks used for keyboards. Incoming might be different if the app has some interesting way of displaying things but since most just throw text on the screen the os has that also. Not much way around that really.

Incoming data can pretty much always be intercepted by the OS. If you write your android app in java (or kotlin), it's trivial for the OS maintainer (or any OEM that modifies it) to inspect your app's "private" memory with reflection.

You could write your app natively, but even then your raw memory can be dumped and analyzed.
